stories.primary_headline: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack

primary_source.headline: Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack
primary_source.content: A drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany, close to Ukrainian cargo planes, on 4 August. It failed to explode as the detonator was apparently faulty, and investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby. A third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the "well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe" and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again. Security experts had speculated that Russia may have been responsible, however Russia has always rejected claims of involvement. Leipzig/Halle Airport in eastern Germany is used by the Germany military and Nato allies for the transport of military goods and also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines - which carries most of the country's aerial cargo. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who was standing beside Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin, said he would order the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the contract for the Russian House in Berlin will also be terminated - which many observers have said has been used for espionage and to spread Russian propaganda.

Germany blames Russia for drone attack on Leipzig airport - CNN

stories.brief: On August 4, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport, a critical hub for German military, NATO allies, and Ukraine's Antonov Airlines, with a second drone suspected of colliding with an aircraft and a third found later, prompting initial suspicions of Russian involvement despite Moscow's denials. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has now officially attributed the incident to Russia, characterizing it as consistent with 'well-established patterns of Russian hybrid operations in Europe.' In a direct response, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and the termination of the contract for the Russian House in Berlin, which has long been suspected of facilitating espionage and propaganda. This decisive action marks a significant escalation in Germany's stance against suspected Russian aggression, signaling a proactive defense against future hybrid attacks and deepening the diplomatic rift, with Dobrindt anticipating further targeting of Germany.

stories.primary_headline: Govt hikes windfall gains tax on petrol, diesel exports; cuts levy on ATF

primary_source.headline: Govt hikes windfall gains tax on petrol, diesel exports; cuts levy on ATF
primary_source.content: New Delhi: The government on Tuesday hiked windfall gains tax on export of petrol and diesel, and reduced it marginally on ATF for the next fortnight.The rate of special additional excise duty (SAED) along with road and infrastructure cess on export of diesel now stands at Rs 25 per litre, up from Rs 24 a litre. SAED on export of aviation turbine fuel (ATF) has been set at Rs 19 per litre, compared to Rs 19.5 per litre earlier.E20 in the sky? Definitely not, says Civil Aviation Minister Naidu, denies rumours of ethanol blend with ATFThe duty on petrol exports has been hiked to Rs 1.5 per litre effective September 1, up from zero earlier.The Finance Ministry in a notification said the duty hikes will be effective from September 1.Amid escalating tensions in West Asia, the Government imposed an export duty on diesel and ATF on March 27 and revised the rate every fortnight.  Beginning May 16,  the levy was imposed on petrol exports.The ministry also said that there is no change in the existing duty rates on petrol and diesel cleared for domestic consumption.Airlines shun Rs 10,000-crore ATF subsidy as fuel prices fallThe windfall tax was levied to increase domestic availability of the fuel amid the war in West Asia.It was also aimed at preventing exporters from taking undue advantage due to price differences as global crude oil prices had increased since the war began.The windfall tax was intended to ensure domestic availability of petroleum products by disincentivising exports amid the West Asia crisis.

stories.primary_headline: CM Vijay can even become US President, says AIADMK chief Palaniswami

primary_source.headline: CM Vijay can even become US President, says AIADMK chief Palaniswami
primary_source.content: Coimbatore (TN): Mocking the ruling TVK's extensive public relations campaigns and Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay's penchant for chartered flights, AIADMK General Secretary Edappadi K Palaniswami on Tuesday sarcastically remarked that the TN CM could even go on to become the President of the United States.Responding to a reporter's query about TVK supporters projecting CM Vijay as a future Prime Minister, Palaniswami deployed heavy sarcasm.Tamil Nadu CM Vijay releases water from Mettur Dam"He could even become the President of America. There is nothing wrong with it, it is his wish," former Chief Minister remarked.However, dismissing the state government's reliance on social media optics, he said, "They are running the government by putting out 'reels' here; that won't work there." He also branded CM Vijay a “costly Chief Minister,” and contrasted the current administration's expenditure with that of former Chief Minister J Jayalalithaa."During Amma's tenure, projects were inaugurated via video conferencing to cut costs," Palaniswami said, mocking the irony of Vijay projecting a humble farmer image while indulging in such expensive travel.Shifting focus to the state's administrative machinery, Palaniswami alleged a complete breakdown in governance.Pointing out that Coimbatore alone had witnessed nearly nine murders in a single month, he stated, "Within 110 days, the law and order situation has completely collapsed. Wherever you look, murders, robberies, and clashes are increasing".The AIADMK leader further accused the Chief Minister of "recklessly announcing schemes" under Rule 110 without fiscal backing.Tamil Nadu CM Vijay announces further hike in milk procurement prices, unveils multi-crore infra pushHe warned that if the state continued borrowing at the current rate, its debt could balloon to Rs 10 lakh crore.Highlighting the steep rise in the prices of essential commodities, including rice, sugar, and cooking oil, he said the government had taken no tangible steps to control inflation.Citing rising corruption and widespread protests by farmers, nurses, and the general public, Palaniswami confidently predicted an early end to the DMK’s tenure. "Looking at all this, this government will not last for five years," he added.

stories.primary_headline: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari lunches 'Arjun Vahini' for early-stage disaster response

primary_source.headline: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari lunches 'Arjun Vahini' for early-stage disaster response
primary_source.content: Kolkata: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Tuesday launched 'Arjun Vahini' for early-stage disaster response, initially comprising 200 personnel, primarily retired soldiers and former Agniveers.Of the 200 personnel, 100 will be deployed in Kolkata, while 50 each will be stationed in the hills and the Sundarbans, he told reporters at the state secretariat."The force will be tasked with responding to disasters and emergencies," the chief minister said.The Sunday Story | The first Agniveers are about to leave. What happens to them next?About their remuneration, Adhikari said the head of the force, 'Veer Nayak', will receive a monthly honorarium of Rs 40,000, while the other members, 'Veers', will be paid Rs 25,000."Their remuneration will increase by three per cent annually," he said, adding that the force will primarily comprise retired soldiers and former Agniveers.In the event of death while on duty, they will be provided Rs 10 lakh compensation, while Rs 5 lakh ex gratia will be paid for permanent disability, the chief minister said.Adhikari added the new force would eventually be developed along the lines of the National Disaster Response Force, with greater manpower and advanced technology to strengthen its disaster-response capabilities.

stories.primary_headline: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay releases water from Mettur Dam

primary_source.headline: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay releases water from Mettur Dam
primary_source.content: Chennai: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay on Tuesday threw open the sluices of the Stanley Reservoir in Mettur, releasing water for irrigation in the fertile Cauvery Delta region after the dam’s water level touched 90 feet. The dam was not opened on its designated date of June 12 due to the non-availability of water, as Karnataka failed to adhere to the monthly schedule of water release stipulated by the Supreme Court.Dressed in a silk shirt and silk veshti, Vijay worshipped the water before showering it with flowers as a mark of releasing water from the dam, which is the lifeline of lakhs of farmers in the Cauvery Delta region comprising Thanjavur, Thiruvarur, Nagapattinam, and Mayiladuthurai districts.Tuesday was chosen for the dam’s opening since the water level reached 90 feet last week — following the established practice that water is released only when the level touches 90 feet to ensure sustained supplies over months. The water level at the dam stood at 91.56 feet, storage at 54.452 tmcft, and the inflow at 10,857 cusecs.Explainer | The Mettur dam and why water released from the reservoir is the lifeline for lakhs of farmers in Cauvery Delta regionThe discharge was increased to 5,000 cusecs at 4:00 PM from 3,000 cusecs at 11:00 AM, and further increased to 7,000 cusecs at 8:00 PM on Tuesday.“Water is being released through the dam powerhouse and tunnel powerhouse. The barrages have been informed to maintain the discharge without any deviation,” a senior government official told&nbsp;DH.Vijay drove from the Salem Airport to&nbsp;Mettur — a&nbsp;distance of 51 kilometers — with people lining both sides of the road to give him a rousing reception. After the event, Vijay visited a farmer's home, met residents near Mettur, interacted with them, gifted a saree to the farmer's wife, and posed for pictures with elderly women.While water from the dam is generally released for the cultivation of&nbsp;kuruvai&nbsp;(short-term crop) on June 12, the schedule could not be maintained this year.&nbsp;Kuruvai&nbsp;has effectively failed in the Delta region, with farmers claiming that paddy was cultivated on only about 2 lakh acres, down from last year’s record cultivation of 6.30 lakh acres.Samba&nbsp;is generally cultivated across an area of about 10.5 lakh to 11 lakh acres in the four districts.The water released from the Mettur Dam will be used for the&nbsp;samba&nbsp;(long-term crop) this year, with farmer associations urging cultivators to adopt direct-sowing methods to save time. The government plans to release about 1 tmcft of water a day for 45 days, relying on the onset of the Northeast Monsoon (NEM) in mid-October to sustain the crop.“Since we need water for the whole season, we are asking our people to sow the seeds directly instead of using the regular cultivation method. We need to conserve water and use the available water judiciously,” P.R. Pandian, general secretary of the Tamil Nadu Cauvery Farmers’ Association, told&nbsp;DH.

primary_source.content:
New Delhi: A citizen of India was among 12 people who were killed in and around the capital of Ukraine in a barrage of aerial offensive late on Monday – around the same time Prime Minister Narendra Modi met President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek and urged him to move from the “endless war” towards the “end of war”. The latest death took the number of Indians killed in the Russia-Ukraine conflict to 58.Russia is in solidarity with Iranian people, Putin tells PezeshkianPresident Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine himself confirmed the death of the Indian in a post on X about the attacks by Russia – targeting Kyiv, Odesa and several other regions of the East European country with drones, ballistic missiles and guided aerial bombs. The Indian was among four people killed in Boryspil, a town outside Kyiv, during the overnight offensive by Russia. In many cities and communities, work to address the aftermath of the Russian attack has been ongoing since last night – nearly 350 first responders are involved in Kyiv and the region alone. A significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the… pic.twitter.com/8cg4ik0V2F&mdash; Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 1, 2026
 

New Delhi’s diplomatic mission in Kyiv also confirmed the death of the Indian. “We are deeply saddened by the tragic death of an Indian national in an attack in Ukraine. The Embassy is in touch with the bereaved family and extends its deepest condolences,” the Embassy of India in Kyiv posted on X. “We are providing all possible assistance for early repatriation of the mortal remains. In this regard, the Embassy is in contact with his company (the employer) and the Ukrainian authorities.” We are deeply saddened by the tragic death of an Indian national in an attack in Ukraine. The Embassy is in touch with the bereaved family and extends its deepest condolences. 1/2 @DrSJaishankar @MEAIndia&mdash; India in Ukraine (@IndiainUkraine) September 1, 2026

The conflict had also killed five Indian seafarers aboard commercial ships in July – four in attacks by Russia and one due to strikes by Ukraine. Two more Indian mariners went missing after an attack by Russia on a cargo vessel near the Port of Odesa in Ukraine. He urged Putin to move away from the “endless war” with Ukraine towards an “end to the war”. “We are moving in this direction,” Putin replied to Modi.

primary_source.headline: Death toll from Russian strike on Ukrainian arms depot rises to 38 - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: The death toll from a Russian strike on an arms depot near the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, has risen to 38, marking the war’s deadliest attack so far this year, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Emergency workers on Sunday continued to extinguish the resulting fires and explosions that began on Saturday in the village of Myla, Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram, adding that bomb disposal teams were also working to clear the site. He said 20 people were injured, while four remained missing. The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv within two months, with officials voicing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas. Separately, Zelenskyy said in a video message that Kyiv is preparing for a new round of talks with representatives of US President Donald Trump, with further details expected on Monday. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine is “doing everything possible to ensure that war does not remain the only option for future developments”, even as Moscow intensifies its strategy of exhaustion.

stories.primary_headline: Pakistan: 21 terrorists killed in clashes with security forces in Balochistan

primary_source.headline: Pakistan: 21 terrorists killed in clashes with security forces in Balochistan
primary_source.content: Islamabad: At least 21 terrorists have been killed in two separate clashes between security forces and rebels in Pakistan's restive Balochistan province, the Pakistan army said on Tuesday.The incidents took place on Monday night in Nokcha, Chagai district and Ziarat Cross, Pishin district, during which five security personnel and one Customs official were also killed, the army said in a statement.It said that twenty-one terrorists belonging to Fitna al-Khawarij were eliminated following effective responses by the security forces.Security forces kill 11 terrorists in various operations in Pakistan's Balochistan, KPKFitna al-Khawarij is a term that the state uses for the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).In the first incident, the terrorists attempted to disrupt the movement of commuters along N-40 Quetta–Taftan Highway by establishing an illegal checkpoint for extortion.&nbsp; “Security Forces responded immediately and, after an intense fire exchange, killed eleven terrorists on the spot,” it said.A large quantity of weapons, ammunition and explosives was also recovered from the terrorists.In the second incident, terrorists launched a coordinated attack in an attempt to breach the Customs House.&nbsp; “Security Forces responded effectively and, after an intense fire exchange, killed ten terrorists,” the army said.The attack on the Customs House was carried out to prevent Customs officials from performing their lawful duties, it added.The army said that five security personnel and a Customs official were also killed during the exchange of fire.Sanitisation operations are being conducted in the surrounding areas to eliminate any remaining terrorists and ensure the safety and security of the local population as well as the vital national highways.Pakistan has witnessed a surge in terror activities, particularly in its Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces in the past few years.The monthly report of the Islamabad-based think tank, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), said on July 31 that the security situation deteriorated most significantly in Balochistan last month.The overall death toll increased by 241 per cent in Balochistan, from 109 in June to 372 in July, the PICSS said.It also said that 62 security personnel were killed in different incidents and operations in Balochistan in July, compared to six killed in June.Security forces, including the military, have been carrying out clean-up operations in Balochistan after a spate of attacks by insurgent groups, especially one incident which saw 27 policemen killed in Ziarat on July 6.

stories.primary_headline: India rejects Hague court order to restore Indus waters pact with Pakistan

primary_source.headline: India rejects Hague court order to restore Indus waters pact with Pakistan - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: India has rejected a ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ordering it to uphold the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, saying the tribunal has no jurisdiction over the matter. India suspended the treaty in April last year after identifying two of three assailants as Pakistani in an attack that killed 26 people at a Kashmir tourist destination. Pakistan denied any involvement in the attack. The standoff places the decades-long conflict over Kashmir as the primary trigger behind the collapse of the historic water pact, pushing a framework that had endured three wars past its breaking point. Under the 1960 agreement, these shared river systems feed 80 percent of Pakistan’s agricultural land. India’s rejection follows the international court’s ruling on Monday that the pact remains fully binding and that India had no justification for ending or suspending it. The tribunal ordered India to limit construction on the Ratle Hydro-Electric Plant in Kashmir, prohibiting work on the dam wall and power intake structure above certain levels. These restrictions will remain in place until 90 days after a World Bank-appointed neutral expert delivers a decision, expected by July 2027. The Indian Ministry of External Affairs, however, said the country does not recognise the court and “categorically” rejected the verdict.

primary_source.content: Rescuers in Nepal are scrambling to save more than 900 workers believed to be trapped underground at hydropower projects following last week’s devastating floods, the country’s disaster management authority has said. At least 933 workers are understood to be stuck in tunnels at about six hydropower projects, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said on Monday. At least 797 people were killed on the border of Nepal and the Chinese territory of Tibet after part of a glacier collapsed in the Himalayas on Wednesday at an altitude of roughly 5,200 metres (17,000 feet) and plunged approximately 1,200 metres (3,900 ft), gathering rock and debris before slamming into the Lhende River in Tibet. The descent and plunge sent water and debris surging downstream into Nepal, creating a lake across the border that overflowed through the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river corridors, destroying several villages. About 3,048 people remain missing. Nepal said on Sunday that at least 781 had been killed on its side of the border, with 2,502 people missing, including 592 foreign nationals. In China, state broadcaster CCTV reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing, including 261 foreigners.

primary_source.headline: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
primary_source.content: The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands. The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future". A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering." The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina. The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim. The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine soldiers.

stories.primary_headline: IIT suicides: Are India’s elite campuses doing enough to protect its students?

primary_source.headline: IIT suicides: Are India’s elite campuses doing enough to protect its students?
primary_source.content: For many students, getting into an Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) is supposed to be the point where years of pressure finally pays off. The ‘IIT’ tag has long been seen as a gateway to a secure future, a good job and a strong career.Inside the campus, however, that promise can look very different."Before coming to IIT, you feel you've given your best," said Piyush, a second-year BTech student at IIT Delhi. "Then you realise everyone here has been the best in their lives."The pressure isn't just exams. It's keeping up with an immensely competitive peer group, managing placements anxiety, and sometimes just finding someone to talk to.IIT Delhi forms fact-finding committee after row over discussion on caste held in campusPiyush, B.Tech II year, IIT Delhi"Before coming to IIT, you feel you've given your best. Then you realise everyone here has been the best in their lives."At least 160 student deaths have been recorded across India's top engineering colleges in two decades, with 69 in the last five alone. A separate RTI data shows 37 suicides across 11 IITs between 2019-20 and 2023-24, with IIT Madras and IIT Hyderabad reporting seven each, and IIT Delhi six.Even these numbers don't tell the full story. No single database tracks the number of student deaths across all 23 IITs. But even then, the issue remains glaring. There is a mental health crisis at India’s premium campuses and despite a number of reforms announced and implemented, it does not seem to be enough.Academic pressure: The first breaking pointFor students like Rohan (name changed), the problem starts long before a crisis."The overall curriculum, the timetable throughout the day is very hectic. And to counter that, there are little to no practical approaches," he said, adding that while the institutes offer yoga sessions, clubs and cultural activities to support student well-being, students often don't have time to take part."If students have to pull all-nighters to accommodate everything they want to do, their personal life, their academics and their social life, then there is definitely a systematic issue,” Rohan, who is pursuing MSc at IIT Delhi, expressed.Piyush described a similar experience. Workload varies sharply between departments, he said, in some, students can balance academics with other things; in others, "you have to keep doing one thing or another."&nbsp;The pressure is, very often, external. “Faculty here have immensely high expectations from students from the very beginning, and students, especially freshers are not used to that pressure. That becomes the breaking point for many,” he added.This is not just one student’s experience.In August 2024, IIT Delhi formed an expert committee to examine student suicides on campus, and recommend reforms in infrastructure and campus environment.The committee highlighted relentless academic pressure, unrealistic deadlines, weekend exams, and a grading system that could reinforce toxic competitiveness. It also flagged caste-based stereotyping, gender discrimination, and faculty-student friction.More importantly, the committee also highlighted a gap in the current mental-health facilities available on campus for students, including distrust in the counselling system.IIT Delhi student’s death | Police file abetment to suicide case against unidentified personsThe said recommendations were reportedly submitted in August 2024. IIT Delhi acknowledged its findings publicly only in April 2025, saying the factors identified had already been recognised internally and that a "comprehensive action plan" was being developed.By then, the institute had already seen another student death, in October 2024.Now, on August 22, 2026, another student has died on the IIT Delhi campus. renewing protests and calls for accountability. The institute has once again set up an inquiry committee, but students are not satisfied.Help is available, but often out of reach?IITs have expanded mental-health infrastructure significantly, including counsellors, psychiatrists, wellness centres, helplines, and peer-support systems. Data from IIT Madras says 3,366 students accessed counselling between 2019 and 2024 and it now offers 24x7 support for students. Similarly, IIT Kanpur has added psychiatrists and weekly psychiatric OPDs.In a recent response to student protest, IIT Delhi said that it has 24x7 counselling services, external mental-health support and an Academic Progress Group to identify students facing academic difficulties.But availability isn't the same as access, say students. "Is the administration here able to provide space for students to reach medical counselling in the first place? No, because there is no time." Rohan said.&nbsp;Piyush, on the other hand, recalled his own first year. "I was completely broken. I experienced anxiety for the first time, and I didn't expect it would become this difficult." He tried to access counselling but couldn't, slots were limited to certain days and times.&nbsp;"When you are mentally okay, you can think, 'There is a counsellor available, I should go talk to them.' But when you are actually struggling, you may not have the capacity to even think about whether someone is available," he said, highlighting that a lot of students often hesitate to approach a counsellor on campus due to fear of judgement and other reasons.Committees keep coming. What changes after them?The IITs, of course, have not been completely passive on the student deaths. After most of the recent student deaths, the administrations have formed inquiry committees and announced support for students as well as victim.Like at IIT Madras, an inquiry committee headed by retired IPS officer G Thilakavathi examined guide-student relationships, academic and personal pressures, support systems and grievance mechanisms after a series of deaths.Its recommendations included giving research scholars greater freedom in choosing guides, allowing students and guides to seek special Doctoral Committee meetings, introducing wellness surveys, providing additional monitoring for students with academic backlogs and strengthening parental support.In the case of PhD scholar Sachin Kumar Jain, a separate inquiry eventually resulted in the suspension of his supervisor, Professor Ashis Kumar Sen.IIT Delhi Director threatens disciplinary action against student protestorsSimilarly, at IIT Bombay, the death of first-year student Darshan Solanki in 2023 prompted an internal investigation and measures including recruitment of dedicated SC/ST counsellors and a committee to examine academic stress among first-year students.Similar committees have been formed across IITs and have recommended similar reforms. A lot of these reforms have been introduced, but gaps still remain.“The question should not be whether there is any infrastructure," Rohan said. "If there is infrastructure, and if you are such a great institute as you claim, why are these issues recurring again and again?” Rohan said.What happened this time?The questions have resurfaced once again, after 31-year-old MSc Physics student Rishikesh Kumar died at IIT Delhi on August 22 after falling from the sixth floor of the Lecture Hall Complex. As per olice reports, no suicide note was found, and the authorities have registered an FIR against unidentified persons on allegations of abetment of suicide.IIT Delhi said Kumar had received treatment and counselling support after concerns were raised about his health earlier this year. He was taken to a specialised hospital for about a month, his semester withdrawal requests were approved and the institute said it continued to provide him support after his return.Rohan*, Msc student, IIT DelhiSoon after the recent incident, the campus was running like nothing had happened... school students were being shown the library.”But students and Kumar’s family raised questions about his return to campus, alleging that he was not given hostel accommodation and faced difficulties in securing an academic project after returning from his medical break. These allegations are now part of the ongoing investigation.The death soon led to protests on campus, with students demanding an independent inquiry into Kumar’s death and alleged administrative lapses.But for students, the concern goes beyond just one incident. “Even after his death, things seemed to go back to normal very quickly, as if nothing had happened,” Piyush, a second-year BTech student, said.Rohan, an MSc student, recalled the days following Kumar’s death, “The campus was running like nothing had happened... school students were being shown the library.”For him, that points to a larger problem, the way repeated deaths can become seemingly normalised, he said.In March 2025, the Supreme Court also set up a National Task Force on Mental Health of Students and Prevention of Student Suicides and mandated to examine academic pressure, discrimination, harassment and institutional accountability.&nbsp;By February 2026, the Ministry of Education reported over 12.88 lakh student responses to its surveys.As students point out, IITs now have counsellors, monitoring systems and helplines in place. The bigger question, however, is whether students can actually access and use these systems when they need them most.

primary_source.headline: Nepal’s glacial collapse foreshadowed a future of climate disaster | Michael Mann
primary_source.content: The deluge capped a summer of extreme climate events, from deadly heatwaves to wildfires. We must take action nowFor millennia, the high peaks of the Himalayas were held together by an invisible, frozen cement – permafrost and glacial ice that bound ancient rock into seemingly unshakable fortresses. But as the planet continues to warm, this alpine glue is liquefying.The glacial collapse and deluge in Nepal and Tibet was not a freak weather event; it was the structural failure of a mountain itself, nature’s latest commentary on the deadly consequences of human-caused planetary warming. And it was the exclamation point on a summer of extremes, illustrating with a sole unnatural disaster the apocalyptic future that lies in store if we fail to take dramatic climate action. primary_source.headline: Firecracker factory blast in India kills 8 children - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: Eleven people have been killed as a firecracker factory in India exploded, leaving many injured and destroying several houses. Three adults and eight children were killed in the accident on Monday. Marking yet another fatal blast at an Indian firecracker factory this year. The youngest child killed was just four years old, according to local police. Several injured people were taken to hospital for treatment. Videos circulated on social media with images of the scene in the aftermath of the explosion in northern India’s Uttar Pradesh state. The footage showed nearby houses completely demolished at the site of the explosion. Other images showed survivors covered in debris and dust. Rescue teams used excavators and citizens employed other tools including stones as they searched for survivors under the rubble. The cause for the explosion was not immediately clear. Local authorities were directed to the scene “to ensure proper treatment for the injured and to reach out to the affected families to provide them every possible assistance”, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said on social media.

primary_source.headline: Journalist Abhishek Upadhyay moves Supreme Court against Ghaziabad police notice seeking X account data
primary_source.content: New Delhi: Independent journalist Abhishek Upadhyay, who claimed to have first reported on the alleged Ayodhya Ram temple donation theft scam, has approached the Supreme Court seeking an immediate stay and quashing of a Ghaziabad Crime Branch notice directing social media platform X to hand over extensive digital information linked to his account.The application, filed in his pending writ petition challenging a Uttar Pradesh police FIR over a road rage incident, assailed a notice of August 22 issued under Section 94 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita by the Crime Branch Investigation Unit, Ghaziabad.Four states move Supreme Court seeking quashing of 116 FIRs over NEET protestsX’s legal team had informed Upadhyay on August 26 that it had received the request concerning his handle.Advocate Anoop Kumar Awasthi mentioned the application before the Chief Justice of India for urgent listing. He submitted that although the FIR relates to an alleged incident of August 18, the police were seeking data from June 1 onwards — the period when Upadhyay collected material for his report on the temple donation irregularities. “If that is disclosed, entire source will be at mercy of state machinery,” he argued.The CJI noted that the court had already granted interim protection against coercive action on the FIR last week and asked why the investigation should not proceed. “What is the problem? We already protected you. They are investigating a matter. Let them investigate,” the CJI observed. The court told counsel to simply file the application, with the CJI adding that the court would examine it.The notice sought login and logout IP addresses, alternate email ID, mobile number, location data including latitude and longitude, device details, IMEI number, name, address, phone number and IP access as well as registration logs. Supreme Court questions Shiv Sena corporator over attack on Kalyan doctors, flags bail concernsUpadhyay contended that the demand is disproportionately broad, risked exposing confidential journalistic sources and could have a chilling effect on press freedom under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.He sought an interim and ex-parte stay on the operation of the August 22 notice and a restraint on authorities from accessing or disclosing any information pursuant to it, apart from its complete quashing.

stories.primary_headline: What should we do with Trump’s monstrous architectural legacy? | Jan-Werner Müller

primary_source.headline: What should we do with Trump’s monstrous architectural legacy? | Jan-Werner Müller
primary_source.content: Questions over Trump’s ballroom and other structures might not feel urgent. But when his reign ends, Trumpism must be repudiatedOn Monday, a majority on the supreme court found a technical way to overrule a lower court’s imperative to stop work, while not taking a stance on whether the whole enterprise might be illegal to begin with. Preservationists, the majority held, appear to lack legal grounds for filing a suit blocking Trump’s ballroom; that means construction will proceed, even if none other than John Roberts, in a dissent, held that “those responsible” were breaking the rules in deciding “what to build up at the People’s House”. The solicitor general, John Sauer, is on record claiming that 65% of the project is completed (of course, he might have exaggerated – such things are known to have happened in Trump administrations). Either way, it is thus likely that there will be a massive structure next to the original White House; and, given that the ruling will embolden the president dramatically to change Washington DC’s landscape by spending money never approved by Congress, we might be cursed with a triumphal arch as well. All of which raises the question: what to do with a monstrous architectural legacy in post-Trump America?Some might dismiss the question as a bit of a luxury problem. After all, a war that also demonstrates the ongoing disempowerment of Congress keeps dragging on; ICE continues its cruel day-to-day work; Trump is trying every tactic to make the midterms go his way. But the built environment, and especially the civic landscape of a capital, is never just an afterthought. Buildings and monuments make values visible, as the philosopher Susan Neiman once put it. And the decision to leave Trump’s structures in place as if his reign had just been another normal era in US history is not neutral – just like leaving Confederate monuments in place is not neutral.Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University Continue reading...

This development is significant because the built environment, particularly civic architecture, visibly embodies national values, and deciding whether to retain these structures in post-Trump America will signal whether his controversial presidency is normalized or its "monstrous architectural legacy" is actively repudiated, much like the debate over Confederate monuments.

stories.primary_headline: Luxembourg drops approval for Israel Bonds issue: What that means

primary_source.headline: Luxembourg drops approval for Israel Bonds issue: What that means - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: Luxembourg is not renewing its authorisation for the issue of Israel Bonds since it expired on Monday, leaving Israel with an uncertain future over its ability to borrow via investors in European markets. Last month, Luxembourg’s Finance Minister Gilles Roth told broadcaster RTL that the financial regulator, the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF), had decided in May not to renew approval for the bond prospectus beyond its August 31 expiry date. A bond prospectus is a legal document that gives investors detailed information about a bond and its issuer before it is launched onto the market. It is produced under the supervision of the financial market within which the bonds are issued – in this case, Luxembourg. Israel Bonds, issued through the Development Corporation for Israel (DCI), are debt securities by the State of Israel that represent a loan from an investor to the Israeli government. Investors earn interest on the bonds they have bought. Capital raised via Israeli bonds is not earmarked for specific purposes but forms part of the Israeli government’s overall financing, which means it can be used to fund defence and military spending. Following the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel and the subsequent launch of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the Israeli government increased its military financing, and Israel Bonds were marketed worldwide as opportunities to “support Israel at War” in the same year. According to Amnesty International, the country raised $4.5bn on international markets through the sale of these bonds between October 2023 and January 2025.

stories.primary_headline: Trump vows to hit Iran hard, says US escorting dozens of ships in Hormuz

primary_source.headline: Trump vows to hit Iran hard, says US escorting dozens of ships in Hormuz - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: United States President Donald Trump has threatened to hit Iran hard and claimed Washington was helping some 30 ships pass through the Strait of Hormuz every night. Trump’s comments on Monday came after the US bombed Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran launched retaliatory strikes targeting US military bases and assets in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, marking the first exchange of fire in more than a month. Speaking to reporters at the Oval Office, Trump claimed the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has blockaded since the start of the US-Israel war in February, was in “extremely good shape”. “We’re taking over. Many, many ships got through last night. As you know, with the navy’s assistance, and we’ve been averaging 30 ships a night,” he said. Earlier, he had promised to respond to Iran’s retaliatory strikes. “We’re going to hit them hard,” he told Fox News. “There will be a response.”

stories.primary_headline: From Bill Gates to Bernie Sanders, most agree the AI arms race is disastrous. Only Europe can make it stop | Alexander Hurst

primary_source.headline: From Bill Gates to Bernie Sanders, most agree the AI arms race is disastrous. Only Europe can make it stop | Alexander Hurst
primary_source.content: An EU export ban on Dutch tech giant ASML’s machines could force the pause we all needAt this point, it should be clear that AI is a choose-your-own-adventure book where every option ends in disaster. Exploding carbon emissions and ecological collapse? Turn to page 37. Other outcomes include some or all of: the bubble bursting and an ensuing financial crisis; mass unemployment via automation; the end of democracy and the rise of authoritarian surveillance states; raving cults who believe the pattern-matching algorithm is a consciousness; terrorists who create devastating bioweapons; nation states that deploy autonomous weapons systems that act on non-human timeframes; nation states or terrorists that hack all the myriad systems we depend on; or an AI that, conscious or not, pursues directives that are at odds with human wellbeing.Imagining that people such as Elon Musk, the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, Palantir’s Peter Thiel and the Trump administration tech adviser Marc Andreessen will lead us to a utopian future of flourishing environmentalism, social harmony and endless leisure requires hallucination and sycophancy so great that that choose-your-own-adventure scenario could only have been written by ChatGPT.Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Over 6,000 Ebola cases confirmed in DRC as death toll nears 3,000

primary_source.headline: Over 6,000 Ebola cases confirmed in DRC as death toll nears 3,000 - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has topped prior surges – becoming the worst the country has experienced – as new data confirms there are now over 6,000 confirmed cases and nearly 3,000 deaths. There is currently no approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which is rapidly spreading across the country. The current Ebola outbreak is “the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic ever recorded”, according to United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as people continue to be infected with the virus faster than frontline workers can track and respond to new cases. This is partly due to many new infections occurring among people who are not being monitored through contract tracing, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. The DRC Ministry of Communications said on social media that 6,041 cases have been confirmed, “including 1,366 recoveries and 2,911 deaths. [Another] 619 patients are in isolation or hospitalised.” The response to the outbreak faces several challenges as cases are mostly concentrated in the eastern provinces of the DRC where densely-populated areas experience insecurity related to armed conflict, displacement and pre-existing humanitarian challenges. The medical charity Doctors Without Borders says existing health needs, as well as airport closures and flight restrictions, are complicating the provision of healthcare, disrupting the flow of staff, diagnostics, referrals and supply chains.

stories.primary_headline: Spain’s Sanchez says Russia, Israel spread disinformation on Ceuta crisis

primary_source.headline: Spain’s Sanchez says Russia, Israel spread disinformation on Ceuta crisis - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has accused Israel and Russia of spreading and amplifying disinformation related to the mass influx of migrants to Ceuta last month, citing research by the European External Action Service (EEAS), the European Union’s foreign service. “After July 30 and 31, rumours and disinformation spread on social networks linked to Russia and Israel, and to an ultra-right international that always uses migration to attack both Spain and Europe and divide it,” Sanchez told Spain’s Cadena Ser radio on Monday. Sanchez said it ⁠was “evident” that the ⁠two countries had used the crisis to criticise ⁠the Spanish government, as ⁠they were at ⁠odds with Madrid over its position on the wars ‌in Ukraine and the Middle East. At least 70,000 people crossed into Spain’s North African enclave from Morocco over several days in late July, triggering a Europe-wide migrant alert. The prime minister also ruled out any responsibility on the part of the Moroccan authorities in the sudden influx of migrants. “No intelligence service with which the Spanish government normally cooperates” had suggested “any … involvement in one way or another of the Moroccan authorities”, Sanchez said.

primary_source.headline: Top officials from Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to meet in Istanbul - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: Turkish officials said on Sunday that the meeting will be attended by foreign ministers, defence ministers, and chiefs of staff from the three nations. According to AFP, the Istanbul meeting will formally establish a “political and defence strategic committee” comprised of such national representatives. Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, quoted by Reuters news agency, said the agenda will cover international security issues, as well as discussions on improving military cooperation and capabilities. The Mecca agreement forms a collective security pact similar to NATO, under which an attack on one member could be considered an attack on all. The alliance was established following the United States-Israel war on Iran. Bangladesh has also stated it is actively considering joining the agreement. The potential expansion is being closely monitored by India, whose Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, told reporters that New Delhi would take all necessary steps to safeguard its national security.

stories.primary_headline: Nepal-China flood disaster: What’s the latest toll, how many are missing?

primary_source.headline: Nepal-China flood disaster: What’s the latest toll, how many are missing? - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: The death toll from devastating floods near the border between Nepal and China has risen to more than 900, with thousands missing following Wednesday’s disaster. Rescue efforts are under way to locate more than 900 missing workers at hydropower projects in central Nepal. Authorities from Nepal and the Tibet region of China have put the total number of missing at just over 3,000, with some bodies washing up in neighbouring India. A glacier collapse high in the Himalaya mountains in Nepal near the border with Tibet triggered Wednesday’s catastrophic flooding and landslides, which buried villages and towns along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems. On Friday, rising water levels in a new lake formed by the build-up of debris prompted a temporary halt to search efforts amid fears of a second flood. Rescue operations resumed after the lake threat was deemed manageable. Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing, said that Chinese authorities say the risk seems to have been reduced, but it has not disappeared.

stories.primary_headline: Iran’s Khamenei calls for Gulf unity as Hormuz tensions persist

primary_source.headline: Iran’s Khamenei calls for Gulf unity as Hormuz tensions persist - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has urged Gulf leaders to identify their “real enemy” and confront it, as Tehran maintains its hard line over the Strait of Hormuz, while regional mediators push for renewed diplomacy. “My emphatic and repeated recommendation to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia and the Gulf, is to identify your real enemy, understand his plan and confront it,” Khamenei said in a message published on Sunday to mark the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad. Khamenei has not appeared publicly since the US-Israeli attacks on February 28 that killed his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The message comes as the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which about 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments passed before the war, remains unresolved. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said on Saturday that Iran had reached an understanding with Oman on a temporary maritime route, but that its implementation would depend on the United States fulfilling its commitments under the memorandum of understanding the countries signed in mid-June, which has since lapsed. “The Strait of Hormuz is closed,” Gharibabadi said, adding that any vessel seeking to cross would have to coordinate with Iran.

stories.primary_headline: Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week

primary_source.headline: Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in southeastern Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week, the world’s nuclear energy watchdog has warned. The plant, which Russia has occupied since 2022, is currently relying on emergency diesel generators, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday. “The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said. The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has not had a delivery from an off-site storage facility in about six months but was supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA said. The Vienna-based agency is now trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines. Zaporizhzhia is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant. It has not generated electricity since September 2022, over six months after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February that year, but the plant’s reactors must be kept cool to prevent a meltdown of the fuel inside.

stories.primary_headline: The home front: How Israel, Iran, and US leaders have been hit by the war

primary_source.headline: The home front: How Israel, Iran, and US leaders have been hit by the war - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: Six months ago, the United States and Israel struck targets across Tehran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other Iranian leaders. It fulfilled a long-held ambition of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a joint attack with the US on Iran, with Washington now locked in a war from which it is unable to extricate itself. Netanyahu might have hoped that the fall of the government in Tehran would be part of his election campaign. And in Iran, the consequences of six months of war have done little to reverse the struggling economy, which appears to be the government’s Achilles heel. The cost-of-living crisis was the mainstay of Trump’s criticisms of the previous administration of Joe Biden during the 2024 US election, but petrol prices alone have risen by 50 percent since the war on Iran began on February 28. “The economic cost of the war is becoming a key issue for many,” Shibley Telhami, government and politics professor at the University of Maryland, told Al Jazeera. Adding to the pressure on Trump are reports that he entered the unpopular war on Iran at the behest of Netanyahu, with fewer than one in three Americans supportive of the conflict, according to a recent Ipsos poll.

stories.primary_headline: Air raids, conscripts and China: How Myanmar’s military is regaining ground

primary_source.headline: Air raids, conscripts and China: How Myanmar’s military is regaining ground - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: The rebel fighters who abandoned Falam in Myanmar in April said they gave up the border town near India only after running out of bullets. The fighters had endured a six-month assault by Myanmar’s military, including hundreds of air strikes and a ground campaign by roughly 1,000 troops. The fall of the town, which had been under opposition control for a year, marked a strategic victory for the military: Falam is home to the only airport in Chin State and commands a trade route to the Indian border. Within weeks, three more towns in Chin had fallen, and by late May, the military was claiming control of the entire northern part of the state. “Falam taught us an important lesson,” said Salai William Chin, a member of the rebel Chin Brotherhood. “Capturing a town and holding it are two very different challenges,” he told Al Jazeera. “Holding it for a long period required manpower, logistics, administration, civilian protection and the ability to withstand repeated attacks, especially from the air.” The retreat is part of a broader reversal across Myanmar. The country’s opposition – a loose coalition of militias and ethnic armed organisations fighting the military that seized power in a 2021 coup – has been weakened. Their gains in 2023 and 2024, when coordinated offensives stripped the military of dozens of towns, have given way to a steady withdrawal from the urban centres they had captured.

stories.primary_headline: Relative of Afghans who aided US military deported to Africa

primary_source.headline: Relative of Afghans who aided US military deported to Africa - Al Jazeera
primary_source.content: The administration of United States President Donald Trump has deported dozens of people to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan whose family members collaborated with the US military, his lawyer and advocacy groups said. The Afghan man, who is in his early 20s, was granted protection against deportation to Afghanistan by a US judge due to fears of persecution by the Taliban, his lawyer, Alma David, said. Advocacy organisations AfghanEvac, a US-based group that assists Afghan allies, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Human Rights First also confirmed his deportation. His family in Afghanistan had received threats from the Taliban, which governs the country, because of his brothers’ involvement in supporting the US military, according to court documents seen by The Associated Press news agency. One of the Afghan man’s brothers lives in the US and served in the Afghan National Army, which collaborated with the US military before the Taliban seized power in 2021, David said. Another brother was a pilot trained by the US and later killed by the Taliban, she added.

stories.primary_headline: Telangana govt staff stage protest over PRC, DA dues, old pension scheme

primary_source.headline: Telangana govt staff stage protest over PRC, DA dues, old pension scheme
primary_source.content: Hyderabad: Telangana government employees staged a large protest at the state secretariat on Tuesday, marking the first visible sign of discontent among government staff, which is notable given that the bulk of the state's expenditure is directed toward welfare schemes.Organized by the Telangana Secretariat Association, the protest saw employees demand the immediate constitution of the second Pay Revision Commission (PRC), prompt disbursal of six pending installments of Dearness Allowance (DA), and the withdrawal of the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) in favor of a return to the Old Pension Scheme (OPS). Telangana police arrest bike mechanic from Bihar for rape, murder of 21-year-old nurseThey also called for the swift clearance of pending bills across various departments. The protest comes against the backdrop of a widening fiscal gap that Telangana needs around Rs 22,500 crore every month to meet its financial obligations but is currently able to generate only about Rs 18,500 crore.Last year, Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy referenced this shortfall while addressing government employees, saying that even if pressed, his government could not raise more than Rs 18,500 crore a month. He questioned whether the state should therefore halt its welfare schemes, and cautioned that protests and hunger strikes at this juncture could risk a complete breakdown of government machinery.

stories.primary_headline: Flood chased me as I ran for 20 minutes, Nepal tunnel engineer tells BBC

primary_source.headline: Flood chased me as I ran for 20 minutes, Nepal tunnel engineer tells BBC
primary_source.content: Pemba Dundu Tamang tells the BBC how he discovered some of his colleagues were missing after he escaped a flooded tunnel It started with a sudden, strong gust of air, says Pemba Dundu Tamang, whose team of about 30 was constructing the tunnel's concrete lining. The blast of wind sent plywood flying through the air and dislodged heavy machinery. Just outside, houses had already been swept away. "I ran towards the tunnel entrance," he said. "The water was chasing behind me and I was running ahead of it." Tamang lost several family members who were at home at the time. Nepal's death toll has exceeded 1,000 after last week's devastating floods, and officials say about 4,000 are missing. A number of the missing - potentially in the hundreds - are labourers like Tamang, working in a vast network of tunnels at hydropower sites along the river. Engineers have been pumping air into these tunnels as part of a huge rescue operation.

stories.primary_headline: GST revenue rises by 14.8% to near Rs 2 lakh crore in August

primary_source.headline: GST revenue rises by 14.8% to near Rs 2 lakh crore in August
primary_source.content: New Delhi: Gross revenue from Goods and Services Tax (GST) rose by 14.8 per cent year-on-year to Rs 1.99 crore in August, driven by a sharp jump in collections from taxes on imports, as per official data released on Tuesday.However, on a month-on-month basis the August mop-up was lower than Rs 2.11 lakh crore revenue recorded in July. The gross GST revenue collection in August 2025 stood at Rs 1.74 lakh crore.GST Council set to meet on September 12; easier registration, automated cancellation likely on agendaNet GST revenue in August, after refunds, stood at Rs 1.68 lakh crore, which is 8.3 per cent higher over Rs 1.55 lakh crore recorded in the same month last year.GST revenue collection from imports surged by 29 per cent year-on-year to Rs 62,604 crore. Gross revenue from domestic transactions increased by 9.3 per cent year-on-year to Rs 1,37,249 crore during the month under review.“This continued outperformance of import-linked tax revenue over domestic collections underscores India's persistent reliance on imported goods and inputs even as domestic demand remains resilient,” said Karthik Mani, Partner, BDO India.Meanwhile, GST refunds jumped 68 per cent to Rs 31,795 crore during the month.The statutory time‑barring deadline of August 31 further strengthened compliance, adding to revenue inflows. Yet, the sharp 72.6 per cent surge in domestic refunds — driven by inverted duty structures — signals a structural imbalance that warrants urgent redressal, said Vivek Jalan, Partner, Tax Connect Advisory Services, a multi-disciplinary tax consulting firm.Jalan said the GST Council may address these anomalies in its forthcoming meeting to ensure that the tax framework supports competitiveness. The GST Council meeting is scheduled to be held in New Delhi on September 12.“The GST Council should consider further easing of the input tax credit restrictions, audit rationalisation and reducing the compliance burden. This would enable businesses to perform better in an increasingly competitive and complex operating environment,” said MS Mani, Partner, Deloitte India.MSMEs in a tax trap: GST rules, delayed payments squeeze India's small firms hardConsidering the fact that the collections have shown a marked increase month on month despite the rate reductions in September last year, the GST Council should consider further easing of the input tax credit restrictions, audit rationalisation and reducing the compliance burden, Mani said.“This would enable businesses to perform better in an increasingly competitive and complex operating environment,” he said.

stories.primary_headline: GoPro to be acquired for $285M, will remain a public company

primary_source.headline: GoPro to be acquired for $285M, will remain a public company
primary_source.content: A company called “Starman Optical” has agreed to merge with GoPro. The deal involves Starman Optical paying GoPro shareholders $1.14 per share, and leaving those shareholders with about 10% of the newly combined company. The deal, expected to close by the end of this year, will wipe away GoPro’s outstanding debt of $92 million. That appears to still be on the cards, as the company said the merger will “maximize the value of GoPro’s IP and growth potential in consumer, commercial and defense markets by recapitalizing the company, strengthening its balance sheet, investing in growth and onshoring the manufacturing of products for strategic markets.” GoPro will also “fully support” its existing consumer products while “investing in growth and a broader, diversified product roadmap.” It’s not exactly clear what all that means, and Starman Optical doesn’t have a significant track record to judge its performance. The company bills itself as an “optical-photonics company focused on the development and domestic manufacturing of optical transceivers and related photonics technologies through its Starman New Photonics business.” Both Starman Optical and Starman New Photonics are part of Starman Holdings, which owns consumer tech brands like Incase, Incipio and Griffin. “Advanced optics and imaging are essential to AI, national security, and the broader economy, yet much of the critical hardware supporting these technologies continues to be manufactured overseas,” Charles Tebele, the CEO of Starman Holdings, said in a statement. “The combination of GoPro’s world-class optical expertise and intellectual property with Starman’s advanced transceiver capabilities and U.S. manufacturing platform creates a unique opportunity. Together, we intend to bring production of these critical components back to the United States.”
